title: Developmental anatomy — DOMiNANCE Originals
source: Obeng's HB2 embryology lectures (F. K. Addai, SMD KNUST)

questions.stem: The complete process of spermatogenesis, from spermatogonium to spermatozoon, takes about
questions.why: Spermatogenesis takes ~64 days: spermatocytogenesis (16) + meiosis (24) + spermiogenesis (24).

questions.stem: Spermiogenesis, the cytodifferentiation of a spermatid into a spermatozoon, takes about
questions.why: Spermiogenesis (tail, acrosome formation, nuclear condensation, shedding of cytoplasm) takes ~24 days.

questions.stem: The blood-testis barrier, formed by tight junctions between Sertoli cells, separates a basal compartment (spermatogonia, mitosis) from an adluminal compartment where
questions.why: The adluminal compartment houses spermatocytes undergoing meiosis, shielded from the immune system by the barrier.

questions.stem: Meiosis in the male occurs only after puberty, which is important because meiotic products
questions.why: Meiotic cells carry novel antigens; the blood-testis barrier plus post-pubertal timing (mature immune system) prevents autoimmune destruction and infertility.

questions.stem: The reserve stem cell of the spermatogenic lineage that can continue spermatogenesis throughout life is the
questions.why: The type A dark (Ad) spermatogonium is the reserve stem cell; type A pale divides to type B, which gives primary spermatocytes.

questions.stem: Primary oocytes are arrested in prophase of the first meiotic division at which stage, from fetal life until puberty?
questions.why: Oocytes rest in the dictyotene (diffuse diplotene) stage of prophase I, held by oocyte maturation inhibitor until the LH surge.

questions.stem: Meiotic arrest of the primary oocyte is maintained by oocyte maturation inhibitor secreted by the
questions.why: Follicular (granulosa) cells secrete oocyte maturation inhibitor (OMI), holding the oocyte in meiotic arrest.

questions.stem: A normal ejaculate volume is about
questions.why: Semen volume is ~1.8-5.5 ml (average ~3.5 ml), with about 100 million spermatozoa per ml.

questions.stem: For fertility, at least what fraction of spermatozoa should be motile with progressive forward movement?
questions.why: At least ~40% of sperm should be motile with forward progression; a minimum of ~15 million per ejaculate is needed.

questions.stem: Immotile sperm flagella due to a ciliary (dynein) defect, as in Kartagener's syndrome, is
questions.why: Primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener's) gives immotile flagella and infertility.

questions.stem: The term for a complete absence of spermatozoa in the ejaculate, even after centrifugation, is
questions.why: Azoospermia is no sperm in the ejaculate; aspermia is absence of semen (no ejaculation).

questions.stem: During the acrosome reaction, the enzyme that digests the cumulus/corona cells around the oocyte is
questions.why: Hyaluronidase digests the corona radiata; acrosin (exposed on the inner acrosomal membrane) helps penetrate the zona; neuraminidase is also released.

questions.stem: Fertilization proceeds in three sequential steps: penetration of the corona radiata, penetration of the zona pellucida, and

options.label: C
options.text: fusion of the oocyte and sperm cell membranes

questions.why: The three steps are corona penetration, zona penetration, then membrane binding and fusion.

questions.stem: Polyspermic fertilization in the human characteristically

options.label: B
options.text: is the usual mechanism of twinning

options.label: D
options.text: dies at or after the 8-cell stage

questions.why: A polyspermic pre-embryo does not proceed beyond a few cleavages and dies around the 8-cell stage.

questions.stem: A hydatidiform mole, with masses of trophoblast secreting large amounts of hCG and no viable fetus, may arise from

options.label: C
options.text: arrest of the oocyte in dictyotene

questions.why: Loss of a pronucleus (often with polyspermic fertilization) gives molar pregnancy with excess trophoblast and hCG.

questions.stem: Cleavage of the human zygote is described as holoblastic, meaning the division furrows

options.label: A
options.text: pass completely through the whole cell

options.label: B
options.text: involve only part of the cell

questions.why: Human cleavage is holoblastic (complete) and occurs without growth, fractionating the zygote into smaller blastomeres.

questions.stem: The ball of blastomeres is moved from the oviduct to the uterus by peristalsis and by

options.label: B
options.text: a ciliary escalator of oviductal cilia

questions.why: Rhythmic beating of oviductal cilia (the 'ciliary escalator') plus tubal peristalsis move the conceptus to the uterus.

questions.stem: Compaction of the morula is driven mainly by
questions.why: E-cadherin tightens cell-cell contacts during compaction and outer-cell polarization precedes the first lineage decision.

questions.stem: The blastocoel cavity forms when outer trophoblast cells pump ions using
questions.why: Outer cells express Na+/K+-ATPase; the resulting osmotic influx of fluid forms the blastocoel, converting morula to blastocyst.

questions.stem: In the morula-to-blastocyst transition, trophoblast fate in the outer cells is promoted by the transcription factor
questions.why: In outer cells the Hippo pathway is inactive, YAP enters the nucleus and activates CDX2 for trophoblast fate; inner cells keep OCT4/SOX2/NANOG.

questions.stem: Pluripotency of the inner cell mass is maintained by the transcription factors
questions.why: OCT4, SOX2 and NANOG mutually reinforce pluripotency in the ICM and suppress trophoblast genes.

questions.stem: Implantation requires a receptive endometrium and a blastocyst that has

options.label: B
options.text: hatched out of the zona pellucida

questions.why: The blastocyst must hatch from the zona to expose the trophoblast to the receptive mid-secretory endometrium.

questions.stem: The three stages of implantation, in order, are
questions.why: Implantation proceeds as apposition, then adhesion, then trophoblast invasion through the epithelial basement membrane.

questions.stem: The usual site of implantation is the

options.label: E
options.text: lower uterine segment over the os

questions.why: Normal implantation is in the body of the uterus, upper posterior wall near the midline; elsewhere is ectopic.

questions.stem: Monochorionic-diamniotic (Mo-Di) monozygotic twins, sharing one placenta but with separate amnions, make up about
questions.why: Mo-Di is the commonest monozygotic pattern (~60-70%); sharing one placenta risks twin-to-twin transfusion.

questions.stem: Monochorionic-monoamniotic (Mo-Mo) twins, the riskiest type, carry a mortality of about
questions.why: Mo-Mo twins (~5% of twins) share one placenta and one amnion, with a mortality around 20%.

questions.stem: Conjoined twinning is possible only in which type of monozygotic twins?
questions.why: Conjoining results from late (post-bilaminar-disc) splitting and occurs only in Mo-Mo twins.

questions.stem: Conjoined twins joined at the cranium are termed
questions.why: Craniopagus (joined at the skull) accounts for about 2-6% of conjoined twins.

questions.stem: The simultaneous presence of two embryos conceived weeks apart in the same uterus is
questions.why: Superfetation is a second conception during an existing pregnancy; it is very rare and almost always linked to ART.

questions.stem: The syncytiotrophoblast differs from the cytotrophoblast in that it is

options.label: B
options.text: the stem layer for the cytotrophoblast

questions.why: The syncytiotrophoblast is multinucleated, amitotic, invasive, in contact with maternal blood, secretes hCG and performs most placental functions; the cytotrophoblast is its mitotic stem layer.

questions.stem: The primary (primitive) yolk sac is lined by a thin layer called
questions.why: Hypoblast-derived Heuser's (exocoelomic) membrane lines the former blastocyst cavity to form the primary yolk sac.

questions.stem: Extraembryonic somatic (parietal) mesoderm is associated with the amnion and chorion, whereas extraembryonic splanchnic mesoderm covers the
questions.why: Somatic extraembryonic mesoderm lines the cytotrophoblast and amnion (with ectoderm); splanchnic covers the yolk sac and allantois (with endoderm).

questions.stem: The umbilical cord develops from the
questions.why: The connecting (body) stalk of extraembryonic mesoderm that suspends the disc in the chorionic cavity becomes the umbilical cord.

questions.stem: The villous chorion related to the decidua basalis, forming the fetal placenta, is the
questions.why: Chorion frondosum (bushy chorion) faces the decidua basalis and forms the fetal placenta; chorion laeve (smooth) faces the capsularis and regresses.

questions.stem: The connective tissue of the umbilical cord that cushions its vessels is
questions.why: The cord vessels are embedded in Wharton's jelly, a mucous connective tissue from extraembryonic mesoderm.

questions.stem: Early in development the umbilical cord contains two arteries and two veins; later there remains
questions.why: One umbilical vein degenerates, leaving the definitive cord with two arteries and one vein.

questions.stem: A chorionic villus becomes a tertiary villus when it acquires

options.label: B
options.text: blood vessels in its mesenchymal core

questions.why: Primary villi (trophoblast) gain a mesenchyme core (secondary), then blood vessels (tertiary), enabling exchange.

questions.stem: Villi that anchor the placenta to the decidua basalis are the
questions.why: Anchoring villi insert into the decidua; terminal (free) villi are the main sites of materno-fetal exchange.

questions.stem: In the mature (late) placenta, the number of layers separating maternal and fetal blood is
questions.why: The late barrier has three layers (syncytiotrophoblast, fused basement membranes, fetal capillary endothelium); the early barrier has six.

questions.stem: Placenta accreta is characterised by

options.label: B
options.text: the placenta overlying the internal os

questions.why: In accreta the decidua basalis is deficient so villi adhere abnormally; percreta is penetration through the myometrium; praevia overlies the os.

questions.stem: At term the normal amniotic fluid volume is about
questions.why: Amniotic fluid rises to ~800-1000 ml near term (it peaks ~1000 ml around 32-34 weeks).

questions.stem: From about 20 weeks to term, the main source of amniotic fluid is
questions.why: By term fetal kidneys make 600-700 ml urine/day (the chief source); lungs add ~250 ml/day; the fetus swallows ~500 ml/day.

questions.stem: After delivery, the placenta normally separates through the
questions.why: Placental separation occurs through the spongy layer of the decidua basalis, aided by a retroplacental haematoma.

questions.stem: The placental hormone with growth-hormone-like actions that promotes maternal lipolysis and glucose sparing is
questions.why: Human chorionic somatomammotrophin (human placental lactogen) has GH-like effects and promotes mammary development.

questions.stem: Gastrulation begins with the appearance of the primitive streak on the
questions.why: The primitive streak appears in the caudal (posterior) three-fifths of the epiblast around day 15-16.

questions.stem: Epiblast cells ingress through the primitive streak by a process called
questions.why: EMT (driven by Snail repressing E-cadherin, with FGF8/WNT) lets epiblast cells detach and migrate through the streak.

questions.stem: The master inducer (a TGF-beta family member) that initiates primitive-streak formation is
questions.why: NODAL induces the primitive streak; WNT3/beta-catenin and FGF8 reinforce streak formation and migration.

questions.stem: The first wave of cells migrating through the primitive streak displaces the hypoblast to become
questions.why: The first wave forms definitive endoderm (also replacing Heuser's membrane); the second wave forms mesoderm; epiblast left behind is ectoderm.

questions.stem: The notochord secretes which signalling molecule to pattern the neural tube and somites?
questions.why: The notochord secretes Sonic hedgehog, induces neuroectoderm (inhibiting BMP) and establishes the midline axis.

questions.stem: The two points where ectoderm and endoderm stay fused with no intervening mesoderm are the
questions.why: Mesoderm surrounds the disc except at the cranial oropharyngeal (buccopharyngeal) and caudal cloacal membranes.

questions.stem: The human embryo has a total of how many pairs of somites?
questions.why: There are 42-44 somites: 5 occipital, 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral and 8-10 coccygeal, appearing days 20-31.

questions.stem: The lateral plate mesoderm is split into somatic and splanchnic layers by the
questions.why: A cavity (the intraembryonic coelom) splits the lateral plate into somatic (parietal) and splanchnic (visceral) leaflets.

questions.stem: The embryonic period of organogenesis, when the embryo is most sensitive to teratogens, spans weeks
questions.why: Gastrulation begins the embryonic stage (weeks 3-8) of organogenesis, a period of high teratogen susceptibility.

questions.stem: Insufficient migration of mesoderm around the oropharyngeal membrane is associated with
questions.why: Deficient cranial mesoderm underlies holoprosencephaly (failure of forebrain cleavage); deficient caudal mesoderm gives sirenomelia.

questions.stem: Caudal dysgenesis with fused lower limbs (the 'mermaid' malformation) from insufficient caudal mesoderm is
questions.why: Sirenomelia (caudal dysgenesis) results from deficient mesoderm around the cloacal membrane.

questions.stem: Remnants of the primitive streak that persist can give rise, in the newborn, to a
questions.why: Failed degeneration of primitive-streak cells can produce a sacrococcygeal teratoma in the buttock region.

questions.stem: New blood vessels forming de novo from angioblasts that differentiate from mesenchyme is called
questions.why: Vasculogenesis forms the first vessels from angioblasts; angiogenesis is sprouting of capillaries from existing vessels.

questions.stem: The primordium of the heart first forms in the
questions.why: The heart primordium forms in the cardiogenic plate (primary heart field) at the cranial end of the embryo.

questions.stem: The single primitive heart tube forms by
questions.why: Two endocardial (heart) tubes move ventrally with folding and fuse into one primitive heart tube.

questions.stem: The cephalic (arterial) end of the bulbus cordis elongates to become the
questions.why: The cephalic bulbus cordis elongates into the truncus arteriosus; from cranial to caudal the tube is bulbus cordis, ventricle, atrium, sinus venosus.

questions.stem: To accommodate elongation, the heart tube bends from left to right forming the
questions.why: The tube folds right to form the bulboventricular (heart) loop.

questions.stem: The superior and inferior endocardial cushions fuse to partition the atrioventricular canal, forming the
questions.why: AV cushion fusion (septum intermedium) divides the AV canal into right and left channels.

questions.stem: The gap between the growing edge of the septum primum and the endocardial cushions is the
questions.why: The ostium primum is the gap below the advancing septum primum; it closes as the septum reaches the cushions.

questions.stem: Before the ostium primum closes, perforations in the septum primum form the
questions.why: Breakdown in the upper septum primum creates the ostium secundum, keeping a right-to-left path open.

questions.stem: The septum secundum differs from the septum primum in that it is

options.label: C
options.text: the floor of the coronary sinus

questions.why: The rigid septum secundum overlaps the free edge of the flap-like septum primum, converting ostium secundum into the oblique foramen ovale.

questions.stem: In the fetus the septum primum acts at the foramen ovale as a

options.label: E
options.text: flap valve allowing only right-to-left flow

questions.why: The septum primum is a flap valve permitting right-to-left atrial shunting in the fetus but not the reverse.

questions.stem: The crista terminalis of the adult right atrium is the persistent
questions.why: Fused venous valves form the septum spurium, persisting as the crista terminalis between smooth and rough right atrium.

questions.stem: Absorption of the right horn of the sinus venosus forms the
questions.why: The right sinus horn is absorbed into the smooth sinus venarum; the diminished left horn becomes the coronary sinus.

questions.stem: The coronary sinus develops from the

options.label: C
options.text: left horn of the sinus venosus

options.label: D
options.text: right horn of the sinus venosus

questions.why: The small left sinus horn becomes the coronary sinus, opening below the sinoatrial orifice.

questions.stem: The smooth part of the left atrium is formed by absorption of the

options.label: E
options.text: right horn of the sinus venosus

questions.why: A single pulmonary vein with four branches is absorbed into the left atrial wall, forming its smooth part; trabeculated tissue becomes the auricle.

questions.stem: The lower edge of the septum secundum seen in the right atrium becomes the
questions.why: The crista dividens (lower septum secundum edge) becomes the annulus ovalis, the rim of the fossa ovalis.

questions.stem: A secundum-type atrial septal defect may arise from excessive resorption of the septum primum or

options.label: B
options.text: failure of the endocardial cushions to fuse

questions.why: Secundum ASD results from too much septum-primum resorption or a septum secundum that cannot cover the ostium secundum, leaving a patent foramen ovale.

questions.stem: The muscular part of the definitive interventricular septum develops from the
questions.why: The muscular IV septum comes from the primary interventricular septum; the membranous part comes from endocardial cushions and bulbar ridges.

questions.stem: The membranous part of the interventricular septum is formed by the endocardial cushions and the
questions.why: Membranous IV septum closure is by the fused endocardial cushions and the proximal truncoconal (bulbar/conus) ridges.

questions.stem: Partitioning of the outflow tract (truncus arteriosus and conus cordis) into aorta and pulmonary trunk is achieved by a spiral septum derived from
questions.why: Neural-crest-derived truncoconal (bulbar) ridges form the spiral aorticopulmonary septum.

questions.stem: Failure of the truncoconal swellings to grow at all, leaving a single outflow vessel over a VSD, is
questions.why: Persistent truncus arteriosus is a single artery arising from both ventricles above a VSD, mixing pulmonary and systemic blood.

questions.stem: Transposition of the great arteries results from the truncoconal swellings failing to
questions.why: Non-spiral (straight) outflow septation gives TGA, with aorta from the right ventricle and pulmonary trunk from the left.

questions.stem: Tetralogy of Fallot arises from a single error in which the conus septum develops
questions.why: An anteriorly displaced conus septum yields a large overriding aorta, stenotic pulmonary trunk, VSD and right ventricular hypertrophy.

questions.stem: A heart that loops to the right as a mirror image, with its apex pointing right, is
questions.why: Dextrocardia (reversed looping) points the apex to the right, often with situs inversus of all organs.

questions.stem: A heart lying partly or wholly outside the thorax, from failure of the sternum to develop, is
questions.why: Ectopia cordis is an externally located heart due to failed sternal fusion.

questions.stem: In the fetus, the vessel carrying the most oxygen-rich blood (about 80% saturation) is the
questions.why: The umbilical vein carries the highest-oxygen blood (~80%) from the placenta; the umbilical arteries carry the most deoxygenated.

questions.stem: The ductus venosus shunts oxygen-rich umbilical-vein blood directly into the
questions.why: The ductus venosus is a high-velocity shunt from the umbilical vein to the IVC, bypassing the hepatic sinusoids.

questions.stem: Oxygen-rich IVC blood is preferentially streamed across the foramen ovale to the left atrium by the
questions.why: The crista dividens (lower septum secundum) and IVC valve direct the oxygenated IVC stream through the foramen ovale.

questions.stem: In utero the ductus arteriosus carries approximately what proportion of right-ventricular output to the descending aorta?
questions.why: About 80-90% of RV output bypasses the high-resistance lungs via the ductus arteriosus into the descending aorta.

questions.stem: The nerve that loops posteriorly around the ductus arteriosus/ligamentum arteriosum is the
questions.why: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the arch of the aorta around the ductus arteriosus/ligamentum arteriosum.

questions.stem: After birth the ductus arteriosus normally closes within
questions.why: The ductus arteriosus constricts and closes within 24-48 hours, becoming the ligamentum arteriosum.

questions.stem: Closure of the ductus venosus after birth is promoted by

options.label: A
options.text: a fall in prostaglandins after cord clamping

options.label: C
options.text: the first breath inflating the lungs

questions.why: Cord clamping and a decrease in prostaglandins close the ductus venosus, which becomes the ligamentum venosum.

questions.stem: At birth the foramen ovale closes because
questions.why: Lung inflation drops right atrial pressure and raises left atrial pressure, pushing the septum primum shut against the septum secundum (later the fossa ovalis).

questions.stem: After birth, the ductus venosus becomes the
questions.why: The obliterated ductus venosus persists as the ligamentum venosum; the umbilical vein becomes the ligamentum teres.

questions.stem: The pharyngeal arches first appear on the embryo during the
questions.why: Five pairs of pharyngeal arches appear as ridges on the ventrolateral head and neck in week 4.

questions.stem: The mesenchyme forming the core of each pharyngeal arch is derived mainly from
questions.why: Arch mesenchyme is mostly neural crest, with a contribution from paraxial mesoderm filling the remaining space.

questions.stem: The external grooves between the pharyngeal arches, lined by ectoderm, are the pharyngeal
questions.why: Clefts (grooves) are external and ectoderm-lined; pouches are internal and endoderm-lined.

questions.stem: The internal outpocketings between the arches, lined by endoderm, are the pharyngeal
questions.why: Pharyngeal pouches are endoderm-lined evaginations of the pharynx, opposite the ectodermal clefts.

questions.stem: Which pharyngeal arch is transient and accounts for the irregular numbering 1,2,3,4,6?
questions.why: The fifth arch is rudimentary and transient, so the arches are numbered 1,2,3,4 and 6.

questions.stem: Each pharyngeal arch is a self-contained module containing a cartilage bar, a muscle group, an artery and
questions.why: Every arch has its own cartilage, muscle, artery and a specific cranial nerve that supplies all of its derivatives.

questions.stem: The nerve of the first pharyngeal arch is the
questions.why: The first arch is supplied by CN V (maxillary and mandibular divisions).

questions.stem: The nerve of the second pharyngeal arch is the
questions.why: The second (hyoid) arch is supplied by CN VII.

questions.stem: The nerve of the third pharyngeal arch is the
questions.why: The third arch is supplied by CN IX.

questions.stem: The fourth pharyngeal arch is supplied by which branch of the vagus nerve?
questions.why: The 4th arch carries the superior laryngeal branch of CN X; the 6th arch carries the recurrent laryngeal branch.

questions.stem: The sixth pharyngeal arch is supplied by the
questions.why: The 6th arch is supplied by the recurrent laryngeal branch of the vagus (CN X).

questions.stem: Meckel's cartilage, the cartilage of the first arch, gives rise to two ear ossicles, namely the
questions.why: The dorsal end of Meckel's (1st arch) cartilage forms the malleus and incus; the 2nd arch forms the stapes.

questions.stem: Besides the malleus and incus, Meckel's cartilage also gives rise to the
questions.why: Meckel's cartilage forms the sphenomandibular ligament; the mandible itself ossifies intramembranously beside it.

questions.stem: The stapes, styloid process and upper part of the body of the hyoid are derived from the cartilage of the
questions.why: Reichert's (2nd arch) cartilage forms the stapes, styloid process, stylohyoid ligament, lesser cornu and upper body of the hyoid.

questions.stem: The greater cornu and lower part of the body of the hyoid bone develop from the
questions.why: The third arch cartilage forms the greater cornu and the lower part of the hyoid body.

questions.stem: The cartilages of the larynx develop from the mesenchyme of the
questions.why: The 4th and 6th arch cartilages form the thyroid, cricoid, arytenoid, corniculate and cuneiform cartilages.

questions.stem: The muscles of mastication are derived from the
questions.why: First-arch muscles include the muscles of mastication, mylohyoid, anterior belly of digastric, tensor tympani and tensor veli palatini.

questions.stem: The muscles of facial expression are derived from the
questions.why: Second-arch muscles include the muscles of facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid and the posterior belly of digastric.

questions.stem: The stylopharyngeus muscle is the sole muscle derived from the
questions.why: Stylopharyngeus (CN IX) is the only third-arch muscle.

questions.stem: Which muscle, derived from the first arch, is innervated by the mandibular nerve and tenses the soft palate?
questions.why: Tensor veli palatini is a 1st-arch muscle (V3); levator veli palatini is a 4th-arch muscle (CN X).

questions.stem: The intrinsic muscles of the larynx are derived from the
questions.why: The 6th arch forms the intrinsic laryngeal muscles; the 4th arch forms cricothyroid, levator veli palatini and the pharyngeal constrictors.

questions.stem: The first pharyngeal pouch gives rise to the auditory (Eustachian) tube and the
questions.why: The first pouch forms the auditory tube, tympanic cavity, inner lining of the eardrum and mastoid air cells.

questions.stem: The palatine tonsil develops from the
questions.why: The endoderm of the second pouch forms the surface epithelium and crypts of the palatine tonsil.

questions.stem: The inferior parathyroid gland and the thymus both develop from the
questions.why: The dorsal 3rd pouch forms the inferior parathyroid, the ventral 3rd pouch the thymus.

questions.stem: The superior parathyroid gland develops from the dorsal part of the
questions.why: Parathyroid IV (from the 4th pouch) migrates less and ends up superior to parathyroid III (from the 3rd pouch).

questions.stem: The inferior parathyroid comes to lie BELOW the superior parathyroid because it
questions.why: Parathyroid III (inferior) is carried caudally by the descending thymus, so it passes below parathyroid IV.

questions.stem: The parafollicular (C) cells of the thyroid are derived from the ultimobranchial body, formed from the
questions.why: The ultimobranchial body (5th pouch), populated by neural crest cells, gives the calcitonin-secreting C cells.

questions.stem: The first pharyngeal cleft (groove) persists in the adult as the
questions.why: The 1st cleft forms the external acoustic meatus and the outer layer of the tympanic membrane.

questions.stem: Overgrowth of the second arch over the third and fourth arches encloses an ectoderm-lined space called the
questions.why: The cervical sinus is normally obliterated; failure to do so leaves a branchial (cervical) cleft cyst.

questions.stem: A branchial (cervical) cleft cyst results from failure of obliteration of the
questions.why: A persistent cervical sinus gives a branchial cleft cyst, typically on the anterolateral neck.

questions.stem: The pinna (auricle) forms from six auricular hillocks that arise from the first and
questions.why: Three hillocks each from the 1st and 2nd arches around the 1st cleft fuse to form the auricle.

questions.stem: Pierre Robin sequence (micrognathia, glossoptosis and cleft palate) is a disorder of the
questions.why: Pierre Robin sequence is a first-arch disorder from underdevelopment of the mandible.

questions.stem: Treacher Collins syndrome (mandibulofacial dysostosis) is characterised by
questions.why: Treacher Collins shows symmetrical underdevelopment of the zygomas, mandible and ears with down-slanting eyes.

questions.stem: Congenital complete absence of the nose is termed
questions.why: Arhinia is the rare congenital absence of the nose; microtia is underdevelopment of the auricle.

questions.stem: The face develops from five facial prominences: a single frontonasal prominence, paired maxillary prominences and paired
questions.why: The five prominences are the frontonasal, two maxillary and two mandibular prominences.

questions.stem: The frontonasal prominence gives rise to the forehead and the
questions.why: The frontonasal prominence forms the forehead, dorsum (bridge) and apex of the nose.

questions.stem: The medial nasal prominences fuse to form the philtrum of the upper lip and the
questions.why: The fused medial nasal prominences form the philtrum and the intermaxillary segment (primary palate).

questions.stem: The alae (sides) of the nose are formed by the
questions.why: The lateral nasal prominences form the alae of the nose.

questions.stem: The lateral parts of the upper lip are formed by the
questions.why: The maxillary prominences grow medially and fuse with the medial nasal prominences to complete the upper lip.

questions.stem: The lower lip and lower jaw are formed by fusion of the
questions.why: The paired mandibular prominences fuse in the midline to form the lower lip, chin and mandible.

questions.stem: A unilateral cleft lip results from failure of fusion between the maxillary prominence and the
questions.why: Cleft lip is failure of fusion of the maxillary prominence with the medial nasal prominence on that side.

questions.stem: An oblique facial cleft results from failure of fusion between the maxillary prominence and the
questions.why: An oblique facial cleft follows the nasolacrimal groove when the maxillary and lateral nasal prominences fail to fuse.

questions.stem: Excessive fusion of the maxillary and mandibular prominences at the angle of the mouth produces
questions.why: Excessive fusion gives microstomia (small mouth); deficient fusion gives macrostomia (wide mouth).

questions.stem: The labial frenulum is a midline remnant of the
questions.why: Ingrowth of the labiogingival lamina frees the lips from the gums; its midline remnant is the labial frenulum.

questions.stem: The floor of the stomodeum is initially formed by the oropharyngeal membrane, which breaks down at the end of week
questions.why: The oropharyngeal (buccopharyngeal) membrane ruptures near the end of week 4, opening the stomodeum into the pharynx.

questions.stem: The primary palate is derived from the
questions.why: The primary palate forms from the intermaxillary segment (fused medial nasal processes) and bears the four maxillary incisors.

questions.stem: The secondary palate develops from palatal shelves that grow from the
questions.why: The secondary palatal shelves grow from the maxillary prominences, elevate above the tongue, and fuse in the midline.

questions.stem: The primary and secondary palates fuse at the
questions.why: The junction of the primary and secondary palates is marked by the incisive foramen.

questions.stem: Cleft palate results when the palatal shelves fail to
questions.why: Cleft palate follows failure of the secondary palatal shelves to elevate above the tongue and fuse in the midline.

questions.stem: The flat bones of the cranial vault (frontal, parietal) form by
questions.why: The membranous neurocranium forms the flat vault bones by intramembranous ossification; the chondrocranium (base) forms by endochondral ossification.

questions.stem: The base of the skull (chondrocranium) is formed by
questions.why: The cartilaginous neurocranium (base) ossifies endochondrally.

questions.stem: The facial skeleton (viscerocranium) is derived mainly from the
questions.why: The viscerocranium (maxilla, mandible, zygoma, nasal bones, ear ossicles) derives from the 1st and 2nd arches.

questions.stem: The anterior fontanelle normally closes by about
questions.why: The anterior fontanelle usually closes around 18 months; premature suture fusion is craniosynostosis.

questions.stem: The mucosa of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue develops from the lateral lingual swellings and the
questions.why: The lateral lingual swellings and the median tuberculum impar (1st arch) form the oral part of the tongue.

questions.stem: General sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is carried by the
questions.why: General sensation of the oral tongue is via the lingual nerve (V3); taste is via the chorda tympani (VII).

questions.stem: Taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is carried by the
questions.why: Reflecting its 2nd-arch contribution, taste from the oral tongue travels in the chorda tympani (CN VII).

questions.stem: The posterior one-third of the tongue develops mainly from the
questions.why: The pharyngeal part forms from the hypopharyngeal eminence (mainly 3rd arch), supplied by CN IX.

questions.stem: The intrinsic muscles of the tongue develop from
questions.why: Tongue muscles arise from occipital myotomes that migrate forward, carrying CN XII with them.

questions.stem: All tongue muscles are supplied by the hypoglossal nerve EXCEPT the palatoglossus, which is supplied by the
questions.why: Palatoglossus is a 4th-arch muscle supplied by the pharyngeal branch of the vagus (CN X).

questions.stem: The boundary between the anterior and posterior parts of the tongue is the V-shaped
questions.why: The sulcus terminalis marks the fusion line; the foramen caecum lies at its apex.

questions.stem: Failure of the lateral lingual swellings to fuse completely in the midline produces a
questions.why: Incomplete fusion of the lateral lingual swellings gives a bifid tongue; a short frenulum gives tongue-tie.

questions.stem: The thyroid gland first develops as a median endodermal thickening at the
questions.why: The thyroid diverticulum arises at the foramen caecum on the floor of the pharynx, linking tongue and thyroid development.

questions.stem: During its descent the thyroid gland remains connected to the tongue by the
questions.why: The thyroglossal duct marks the descent path; it normally degenerates, leaving the foramen caecum as a remnant.

questions.stem: The thyroid reaches its final position anterior to the trachea, below the cricoid, by about week
questions.why: By the 7th week the thyroid lies in its definitive position below the cricoid cartilage.

questions.stem: A thyroid that fails to descend and remains at the back of the tongue is a
questions.why: Failure of descent leaves a lingual thyroid at the foramen caecum region.

questions.stem: A persistent remnant of the thyroglossal duct that accumulates fluid in the midline neck is a
questions.why: A thyroglossal cyst is a midline neck swelling from a persistent thyroglossal duct remnant.

questions.stem: Tooth development (odontogenesis) results from interaction between oral ectoderm and mesenchyme derived from
questions.why: Teeth form from oral ectoderm and neural-crest-derived ectomesenchyme, beginning about week 6.

questions.stem: The enamel organ, which gives rise to ameloblasts, is derived from
questions.why: The ectodermal enamel organ forms ameloblasts and hence enamel; the mesenchymal dental papilla forms dentine and pulp.

questions.stem: Dentine and the dental pulp are formed from the
questions.why: The dental papilla (mesenchyme) forms odontoblasts (dentine) and the pulp; the dental follicle forms cementum, PDL and alveolar bone.

questions.stem: Cementum, the periodontal ligament and alveolar bone all develop from the
questions.why: The dental follicle (sac) gives rise to cementum, periodontal ligament and alveolar bone.

questions.stem: Enamel cannot be regenerated after tooth eruption because
questions.why: Ameloblasts are lost once the tooth erupts, so enamel cannot be replaced; odontoblasts persist, so dentine can be.

questions.stem: The deciduous (primary) dentition consists of how many teeth?
questions.why: There are 20 deciduous teeth (10 per jaw) and 32 permanent teeth (16 per jaw).

questions.stem: Which stage of tooth development shows the enamel organ with a dental papilla and dental follicle first recognisable?
questions.why: At the cap stage the enamel organ, dental papilla and dental follicle first become distinguishable.

questions.stem: The respiratory primordium first appears in week 4 as the
questions.why: A laryngotracheal (respiratory) groove appears on the ventral wall of the foregut in week 4 and grows into the laryngotracheal diverticulum.

questions.stem: The laryngotracheal tube is separated from the oesophagus by the
questions.why: The tracheoesophageal (laryngotracheal) septum divides the foregut into a ventral laryngotracheal tube and a dorsal oesophagus.

questions.stem: The epithelium lining the trachea, bronchi and alveoli is derived from
questions.why: Respiratory epithelium (and glands) arise from foregut endoderm; the cartilage, smooth muscle and connective tissue come from splanchnic mesoderm.

questions.stem: The cartilage and smooth muscle of the respiratory tree are derived from
questions.why: Splanchnic (visceral) mesoderm forms the cartilage, smooth muscle and connective tissue around the endodermal airway.

questions.stem: An incompletely formed tracheoesophageal septum results in a
questions.why: Imperfect partitioning of the foregut gives a tracheoesophageal fistula, often with oesophageal atresia.

questions.stem: Inhaled foreign objects lodge more often in the right main bronchus because it is
questions.why: The right main bronchus is wider and more vertical, so aspirated material tends to enter it.

questions.stem: During lung development the right lung is supplied by how many lobar (secondary) bronchi?
questions.why: The right main bronchus divides into three lobar bronchi, the left into two, matching the lung lobes.

questions.stem: During which phase of lung development does the air-blood barrier first begin to form?
questions.why: In the canalicular phase the respiratory portion differentiates and capillaries approach the epithelium, setting up the air-blood barrier.

questions.stem: Type I pneumocytes (thin squamous cells) first differentiate during the
questions.why: In the saccular phase the epithelium thins into type I pneumocytes, establishing terminal air sacs for gas exchange.

questions.stem: Surfactant-producing type II pneumocytes begin to differentiate from about
questions.why: Type II pneumocytes appear from about 28 weeks; a baby born at 28 weeks has a chance of surviving unaided.

questions.stem: Respiratory distress syndrome (hyaline membrane disease) of the newborn is caused by
questions.why: Lack of surfactant raises alveolar surface tension, causing RDS, common in preterm infants.

questions.stem: Before birth, gas exchange for the fetus is carried out by the
questions.why: The placenta is the respiratory organ until birth; the lungs develop structurally without functioning.

questions.stem: A markedly reduced volume of amniotic fluid (oligohydramnios) is associated with
questions.why: Oligohydramnios restricts lung expansion and fetal breathing movements, causing hypoplastic lungs.

questions.stem: Fetal breathing movements, which condition the respiratory muscles, begin at about
questions.why: Rhythmic fetal breathing movements using amniotic fluid are seen from about 20-21 weeks.

questions.stem: The embryonic body cavities all arise from the
questions.why: The pericardial, pleural and peritoneal cavities all derive from the intraembryonic coelom in the lateral plate mesoderm.

questions.stem: Cavitation of the lateral plate mesoderm splits it into a somatic layer and a
questions.why: The intraembryonic coelom splits lateral mesoderm into somatic (parietal) and splanchnic (visceral) layers.

questions.stem: The pleural and pericardial cavities are separated from each other by the
questions.why: The pleuropericardial folds grow in as the lungs expand and fuse to separate the pleural and pericardial cavities.

questions.stem: The pleuropericardial folds carry which two structures?

options.label: B
options.text: the splanchnic nerves and the SMA

options.label: D
options.text: the vagus nerve and the aorta

options.label: E
options.text: the thoracic duct and azygos vein

questions.why: The pleuropericardial folds contain the common cardinal veins and the phrenic nerve.

questions.stem: The fused pleuropericardial membranes form the
questions.why: The dorsally fused pleuropericardial membranes become the fibrous pericardium.

questions.stem: The right pleuropericardial opening closes before the left because

options.label: B
options.text: the heart descends to the left

options.label: C
options.text: the right phrenic nerve is shorter

options.label: D
options.text: the left horn forms the coronary sinus

options.label: E
options.text: the right common cardinal vein is larger

questions.why: The larger right common cardinal vein produces a larger membrane, so the right canal closes first.

questions.stem: The central tendon of the diaphragm is derived from the
questions.why: The septum transversum forms the central tendon; the crura come from the dorsal oesophageal mesentery and the muscle from the body wall and myotomes.

questions.stem: The crura of the diaphragm develop from the
questions.why: The dorsal mesentery of the oesophagus gives rise to the crura of the diaphragm.

questions.stem: The muscle of the diaphragm is innervated by the phrenic nerve, reflecting its origin from myotomes of segments
questions.why: Myoblasts from cervical somites C3-C5 migrate into the septum transversum, carrying the phrenic nerve (C3,4,5).

questions.stem: The pleural and peritoneal cavities are separated by the
questions.why: The pleuroperitoneal membranes grow in and fuse with the septum transversum and oesophageal mesentery by the end of week 6.

questions.stem: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia most often occurs on the left posterolateral side because

options.label: A
options.text: the liver blocks the right side

options.label: C
options.text: the stomach is on the left

questions.why: The left pleuroperitoneal canal (foramen of Bochdalek) closes later than the right, so herniation is commoner on the left.

questions.stem: The lung on the side of a congenital diaphragmatic hernia characteristically shows
questions.why: Abdominal viscera herniating into the chest compress the developing lung, causing pulmonary hypoplasia.

questions.stem: The primitive gut tube is formed from the
questions.why: Embryonic folding incorporates the roof of the secondary yolk sac as the primitive gut (foregut, midgut, hindgut).

questions.stem: The cranial limit of the foregut is marked by the
questions.why: The buccopharyngeal (oropharyngeal) membrane is the cranial limit; the cloacal membrane is the caudal limit of the hindgut.

questions.stem: The artery of the midgut is the
questions.why: The foregut is supplied by the coeliac trunk, the midgut by the superior mesenteric artery and the hindgut by the inferior mesenteric artery.

questions.stem: The muscle in the upper third of the oesophagus is
questions.why: Splanchnic mesoderm gives striated muscle in the upper third, smooth muscle in the lower third and a mixture in the middle.

questions.stem: Oesophageal atresia and stenosis are thought to result from

options.label: B
options.text: failure of the vitelline duct to close

options.label: E
options.text: failure of recanalisation of the lumen

questions.why: The oesophageal lumen is temporarily occluded by epithelium; failure to recanalise gives stenosis or atresia.

questions.stem: The stomach first appears during week 4 as a fusiform dilatation of the
questions.why: The stomach begins as a fusiform swelling of the foregut caudal to the oesophagus in week 4.

questions.stem: The stomach rotates 90 degrees clockwise about its longitudinal axis, which explains why the

options.label: B
options.text: left vagus supplies the anterior wall

options.label: C
options.text: right vagus supplies the anterior wall

options.label: D
options.text: left vagus supplies the lesser curvature

questions.why: After the 90 degrees clockwise rotation the left vagus comes to lie on the anterior wall and the right vagus on the posterior wall.

questions.stem: The greater curvature of the stomach forms because its dorsal border

options.label: B
options.text: is tethered by the lesser omentum

options.label: C
options.text: grows faster than the ventral border

questions.why: The posterior (dorsal) wall grows faster than the anterior, producing the greater curvature.

questions.stem: The omental bursa (lesser sac) forms behind the stomach as a consequence of
questions.why: The 90 degrees longitudinal rotation of the stomach draws the dorsal mesogastrium behind it to create the omental bursa.

questions.stem: Congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis classically presents with
questions.why: Hypertrophy of the pyloric circular muscle causes projectile non-bilious vomiting at 3-6 weeks, typically in firstborn males.

questions.stem: Growth of the liver into the ventral mesentery divides it into the falciform ligament and the
questions.why: The liver splits the ventral mesentery into the lesser omentum (liver to stomach) and the falciform ligament (liver to body wall).

questions.stem: The spleen develops within the
questions.why: The spleen arises in the mesenchyme of the dorsal mesogastrium, splitting it into the gastrosplenic and lienorenal ligaments.

questions.stem: The ligament connecting the spleen to the posterior body wall at the kidney is the
questions.why: The dorsal mesogastrium forms the gastrosplenic (spleen to stomach) and lienorenal (spleen to kidney) ligaments.

questions.stem: The free margin of the lesser omentum (hepatoduodenal ligament) contains the
questions.why: The hepatoduodenal ligament carries the portal triad (bile duct, portal vein and hepatic artery) and roofs the epiploic foramen.

questions.stem: The liver develops as the hepatic bud, an outgrowth of the foregut that grows into the
questions.why: The hepatic bud grows into the septum transversum, whose mesenchyme forms the liver's connective tissue and capsule.

questions.stem: The hepatocytes of the liver are derived from
questions.why: Endodermal cells of the hepatic bud form hepatocytes; the septum transversum mesenchyme forms the connective tissue and capsule.

questions.stem: The gallbladder and cystic duct develop from the
questions.why: A cystic bud off the hepatic diverticulum expands into the gallbladder, its stalk becoming the cystic duct.

questions.stem: The uncinate process and lower part of the head of the pancreas develop from the
questions.why: The ventral bud migrates posteriorly and forms the uncinate process and lower head; the dorsal bud forms the upper head, body and tail.

questions.stem: The superior mesenteric artery comes to lie anterior to the uncinate process because of
questions.why: As the ventral pancreatic bud swings posteriorly around the duodenum, the SMA ends up behind the pancreatic body but in front of the uncinate process.

questions.stem: The midgut extends from the opening of the bile duct to the
questions.why: The midgut runs from the entry of the bile duct into the duodenum to the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon.

questions.stem: Physiological herniation of the midgut into the umbilical cord occurs during week
questions.why: Around week 6 the rapidly elongating midgut loop herniates into the umbilical cord because the abdominal cavity is too small.

questions.stem: During its development the midgut loop rotates a total of
questions.why: The midgut rotates 270 degrees counter-clockwise around the superior mesenteric artery (90 while herniated, 180 on return).

questions.stem: The caecum and appendix develop from the

options.label: E
options.text: cranial limb of the midgut loop

questions.why: The caecal (caecal swelling) diverticulum on the midgut loop forms the caecum and appendix.

questions.stem: Failure of the herniated midgut loop to return to the abdomen, leaving viscera in a sac covered by amnion, is
questions.why: Omphalocoele (exomphalos) is persistence of the physiological hernia; the sac is covered by amnion and peritoneum.

questions.stem: Gastroschisis differs from omphalocoele in that the herniated bowel

options.label: E
options.text: is not covered by a membrane

questions.why: In gastroschisis the viscera protrude through a full-thickness body wall defect (usually right of the umbilicus) with no covering sac.

questions.stem: Meckel's diverticulum is a persistent remnant of the
questions.why: Meckel's diverticulum is a vestige of the vitelline duct, found in the distal ileum; it may contain ectopic gastric or pancreatic tissue.

questions.stem: The hindgut gives rise to the descending colon, sigmoid colon, rectum and the

options.label: B
options.text: upper two-thirds of the anal canal

options.label: C
options.text: lower third of the anal canal

questions.why: The hindgut forms the distal third of the transverse colon through to the upper two-thirds of the anal canal; its artery is the IMA.

questions.stem: The cloaca is partitioned into a urogenital sinus and a rectoanal canal by the
questions.why: The urorectal septum grows down to meet the cloacal membrane, dividing the cloaca and forming the perineal body at the point of fusion.

questions.stem: The lower one-third of the anal canal (below the pectinate line) is derived from
questions.why: Below the pectinate line the anal canal arises from the ectodermal proctodeum; above it from hindgut endoderm.

questions.stem: Above the pectinate line the anal canal is supplied by the superior rectal artery, a branch of the
questions.why: Above the pectinate line (hindgut) the blood supply is the superior rectal artery from the IMA; below it the inferior rectal artery from the internal iliac.

questions.stem: Below the pectinate line the anal canal is sensitive to pain because it is supplied by the
questions.why: The lower anal canal has somatic innervation from the inferior rectal branch of the pudendal nerve and is pain-sensitive; the upper part is not.

questions.stem: Hirschsprung disease (congenital aganglionic megacolon) results from failure of migration of
questions.why: Neural-crest-derived parasympathetic ganglion cells fail to populate the myenteric plexus of the distal colon, which cannot relax.

questions.stem: Imperforate anus and rectal fistulas arise mainly from abnormal development of the
questions.why: Faulty partitioning of the cloaca by the urorectal septum underlies imperforate anus and rectourinary/rectovaginal fistulas.

questions.stem: The neonate's first stool, a sticky greenish-black material, is called
questions.why: Meconium is the first stool, composed of swallowed amniotic fluid, bile, mucus and shed cells; it is normally passed within 24-48 hours.

questions.stem: The kidneys and ureters develop from which germ layer derivative?
questions.why: The nephrogenic cord of intermediate mesoderm gives rise to the uriniferous tubules; the bladder is endodermal.

questions.stem: The three successive kidney systems that develop in the embryo are the pronephros, mesonephros and
questions.why: Three sets form in cranio-caudal succession: pronephros, mesonephros and the definitive metanephros.

questions.stem: The pronephros appears in the cervical region during week 4 and is
questions.why: The pronephros is rudimentary and soon regresses, but it induces the mesonephros.

questions.stem: The duct that drains the mesonephros is the
questions.why: Mesonephric tubules drain into the mesonephric (Wolffian) duct, which reaches the cloaca.

questions.stem: In the male, a few mesonephric tubules persist as the functional
questions.why: Surviving mesonephric tubules form the efferent ductules of the testis; non-functional remnants form aberrant ductules and the appendix of the epididymis.

questions.stem: Remnants of the mesonephric tubules in the female form the vestigial epoophoron and
questions.why: In females the mesonephric tubules persist as the epoophoron and paroophoron; the mesonephric duct may persist as Gartner's cyst.

questions.stem: The definitive metanephros (permanent kidney) is formed by the metanephric blastema and the
questions.why: The metanephros arises from the ureteric bud (a diverticulum of the mesonephric duct) and the surrounding metanephric blastema.

questions.stem: The ureteric bud gives rise to the ureter, renal pelvis, calyces and the
questions.why: The ureteric bud forms the collecting system (ureter, pelvis, calyces, collecting ducts); the metanephric blastema forms the nephrons.

questions.stem: The nephrons (from glomerulus to distal convoluted tubule) are derived from the
questions.why: Metanephric blastema (cap) forms the excretory units (nephrons); the ureteric bud forms the collecting system.

questions.stem: Failure of a metanephric vesicle to connect with the collecting system may produce a
questions.why: A vesicle that does not join the collecting duct cannot drain and becomes a cyst.

questions.stem: The permanent kidney first forms in the pelvis and then ascends to lie opposite the
questions.why: The kidney ascends from the pelvis to the upper lumbar region, reaching about L2.

questions.stem: During ascent the kidney is supplied in turn by progressively higher branches of the aorta; a persisting lower vessel is an
questions.why: Lower arteries are normally abandoned during ascent; one that persists becomes an accessory or aberrant renal artery.

questions.stem: As it ascends, the kidney rotates about its longitudinal axis so that the hilum comes to face
questions.why: The kidney rotates 90 degrees medially, bringing the renal pelvis and hilum to face medially.

questions.stem: A kidney that fails to ascend and remains in the pelvis is a
questions.why: Failure of ascent gives a pelvic (ectopic) kidney.

questions.stem: A horseshoe kidney becomes trapped during ascent at the
questions.why: Fusion of the lower poles gives a horseshoe kidney, whose ascent is arrested by the root of the inferior mesenteric artery.

questions.stem: Double or bifid ureters arise from an abnormality of the
questions.why: Premature or complete division of the ureteric bud produces bifid or double ureters.

questions.stem: The urinary bladder develops mainly from the
questions.why: The bladder forms from the vesical (upper) part of the urogenital sinus, which is continuous with the allantois; its epithelium is endodermal.

questions.stem: The epithelium lining the urinary bladder is derived from
questions.why: Bladder epithelium is endodermal (from the urogenital sinus); the muscle and connective tissue come from splanchnic mesoderm.

questions.stem: The trigone of the bladder is formed by incorporation of the
questions.why: Absorption of the caudal mesonephric ducts into the bladder wall forms the trigone.

questions.stem: After birth the obliterated allantois (urachus) persists as the
questions.why: The urachus fibroses into the median umbilical ligament running from the bladder apex to the umbilicus.

questions.stem: Persistence of the urachal lumen giving urine discharge at the umbilicus is a
questions.why: A fully patent urachus connects bladder to umbilicus; partial persistence gives a urachal cyst, sinus or diverticulum.

questions.stem: Exstrophy of the bladder, in which the bladder opens onto the lower abdominal wall, is due to failure of
questions.why: Deficient migration of mesoderm around the cloacal membrane leaves the anterior bladder and abdominal wall open, often with epispadias.

questions.stem: The genetic (chromosomal) sex of the embryo is determined
questions.why: Genetic sex is set at fertilisation by the sex chromosome of the spermatozoon (X or Y).

questions.stem: The gene on the Y chromosome that triggers testis formation is
questions.why: The SRY gene encodes testis-determining factor (TDF), which drives the indifferent gonad toward a testis.

questions.stem: Until about week 7 the gonads are described as
questions.why: The gonadal ridges are bipotential until the 7th week, when SRY (or its absence) decides their fate.

questions.stem: Primordial germ cells first arise in the
questions.why: PGCs differentiate in the yolk-sac endoderm near the allantois and migrate to the gonadal ridge via the dorsal mesentery.

questions.stem: Primordial germ cells reach the gonadal ridge by migrating along the
questions.why: PGCs migrate from the yolk sac through the dorsal mesentery into the gonadal ridges during weeks 4-6.

questions.stem: The gonadal (genital) ridge arises on the medial side of the
questions.why: The gonadal ridge forms from proliferation of mesenchyme and coelomic epithelium medial to the mesonephros.

questions.stem: In the testis, the Sertoli cells are derived from the
questions.why: Sex cord cells become Sertoli cells; the PGCs become spermatogonia and the interstitial mesenchyme forms Leydig cells.

questions.stem: Testosterone is first produced in the fetal testis by the
questions.why: Interstitial (Leydig) cells arise from gonadal mesenchyme and begin producing testosterone by about week 8.

questions.stem: Anti-Mullerian hormone (Mullerian inhibiting substance) is secreted by the
questions.why: Sertoli cells secrete AMH/MIH, which causes regression of the paramesonephric (Mullerian) ducts in the male.

questions.stem: In the absence of SRY the gonad develops into an ovary, driven by
questions.why: Without SRY, WNT4 acting via DAX1 steers the bipotential gonad toward an ovary.

questions.stem: Oogonia enter meiosis and arrest as primary oocytes in
questions.why: Primary oocytes become arrested in prophase I of meiosis until puberty (the follicular cells secrete oocyte maturation inhibitor).

questions.stem: The number of primordial follicles is maximal at about
questions.why: About 7 million follicles exist at 5 months, falling to about 2 million at birth and 40,000 by puberty.

questions.stem: The male genital ducts (epididymis, vas deferens, ejaculatory duct) develop from the
questions.why: Under testosterone the mesonephric ducts form the epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicle and ejaculatory duct.

questions.stem: The uterine tubes, uterus and upper vagina develop from the
questions.why: The paramesonephric ducts form the uterine tubes, uterus, cervix and upper vagina when MIH is absent.

questions.stem: Virilisation of the mesonephric ducts into male genital ducts is driven by
questions.why: Testosterone from Leydig cells stimulates the mesonephric ducts to form the male duct system.

questions.stem: In the male, the paramesonephric ducts regress, leaving the appendix of the testis and the
questions.why: Mullerian remnants in the male are the appendix of the testis and the prostatic utricle.

questions.stem: A remnant of the mesonephric duct persisting in the wall of the female genital tract is
questions.why: The mesonephric duct may persist in the female as Gartner's duct/cyst alongside the vagina.

questions.stem: The lower one-third of the vagina is derived from the
questions.why: The upper vagina forms from the paramesonephric ducts; the lower part forms from the sinovaginal bulbs/vaginal plate of the urogenital sinus.

questions.stem: The broad ligament of the uterus is formed as the fusing paramesonephric ducts drag a fold of
questions.why: The midline fusion of the paramesonephric ducts pulls a transverse peritoneal fold across the pelvis, forming the broad ligament.

questions.stem: Complete failure of fusion of the paramesonephric ducts produces a
questions.why: Total non-fusion gives a double uterus and often double vagina (uterus didelphys).

questions.stem: Persistence of the midline septum between the fused paramesonephric ducts gives a
questions.why: Failure to resorb the median septum after fusion leaves a septate uterus.

questions.stem: The external genitalia develop from primordia that are indifferent until about week
questions.why: The external genitalia arise from common primordia and remain indifferent until about week 12.

questions.stem: The genital tubercle gives rise to the glans penis in the male and the
questions.why: The genital tubercle becomes the glans of the penis in males and the clitoris in females.

questions.stem: The labioscrotal (genital) swellings form the scrotum in the male and the
questions.why: Labioscrotal swellings fuse to form the scrotum in males and remain separate as the labia majora in females.

questions.stem: The urethral folds form the labia minora in the female and, in the male, the
questions.why: The urethral folds fuse over the urethral groove to form the penile urethra in males and remain as labia minora in females.

questions.stem: Differentiation of the male EXTERNAL genitalia depends specifically on
questions.why: DHT (from testosterone via 5-alpha-reductase) drives masculinisation of the external genitalia; the internal ducts need testosterone itself.

questions.stem: Hypospadias, in which the urethra opens on the ventral surface of the penis, results from failure of fusion of the
questions.why: Incomplete fusion of the urethral folds leaves the urethral opening on the underside of the penis.

questions.stem: The fibromuscular cord that guides descent of the gonad to the scrotum or labia is the
questions.why: The gubernaculum extends from the lower pole of the gonad to the labioscrotal swelling and guides its descent.

questions.stem: Indirect inguinal hernias are commoner on the right side because

options.label: B
options.text: the gubernaculum is longer on the right

options.label: C
options.text: the processus closes first on the left

questions.why: The left testis descends slightly earlier, so the right processus vaginalis tends to remain patent a little longer.

questions.stem: The tunica vaginalis covering the testis is derived from the
questions.why: The tunica vaginalis is formed from the processus vaginalis, an evagination of peritoneum.

questions.stem: As the testis descends it acquires the internal spermatic fascia from the
questions.why: Internal spermatic fascia comes from transversalis fascia, cremasteric from internal oblique and external spermatic from external oblique aponeurosis.

questions.stem: Undescended testis (cryptorchidism), if bilateral and untreated, leads to
questions.why: Higher intra-abdominal temperature destroys spermatogonia, so bilateral cryptorchidism causes infertility; Leydig cells are spared.

questions.stem: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia in a 46,XX fetus causes virilisation because of

options.label: D
options.text: a defect in the androgen receptor

questions.why: A 21-hydroxylase deficiency shunts adrenal steroids into androgens, masculinising the external genitalia of a genetic female.

questions.stem: In complete androgen insensitivity syndrome (46,XY) the external genitalia are female because
questions.why: Testes and testosterone are present, but target cells cannot respond to androgens, so external genitalia develop along the female pattern.

questions.stem: A 46,XY individual with female-appearing genitalia at birth who virilises at puberty ('guevedoces') typically has
questions.why: 5-alpha-reductase deficiency gives low DHT (female-type external genitalia at birth) but rising testosterone virilises them at puberty.

questions.stem: In complete androgen insensitivity syndrome, the uterus and uterine tubes are absent because
questions.why: Functioning Sertoli cells secrete AMH, so the Mullerian ducts regress even though the ducts cannot respond to androgens.

questions.stem: The central nervous system develops from the
questions.why: The CNS arises from the neural plate, a thickening of ectoderm (neuroectoderm) that appears in week 3.

questions.stem: The process by which the neural plate folds and closes into the neural tube is
questions.why: Neurulation is the folding of the neural plate into the neural tube.

questions.stem: Formation of the neural plate is induced by signals from the notochord and
questions.why: The notochord and paraxial mesoderm release factors that induce overlying ectoderm to become neural plate.

questions.stem: Besides the neural tube, neurulation also gives rise to the surface epidermis and the
questions.why: Ectoderm forms the neural tube, the neural crest and the epidermis of the skin.

questions.stem: The forebrain and midbrain are induced in ectoderm where BMP4 is inhibited by
questions.why: Noggin, chordin and follistatin inhibit BMP4 to permit forebrain-midbrain fate; WNT3a/FGF/retinoic acid permit hindbrain-spinal cord fate.

questions.stem: Which is NOT a derivative of neural crest cells?
questions.why: Neural crest forms melanocytes, sensory and autonomic ganglia, Schwann cells, adrenal medulla and much craniofacial tissue; limb muscle is from somites.

questions.stem: The adrenal (suprarenal) medulla is derived from
questions.why: Chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla are neural crest derivatives; the cortex is from mesoderm.

questions.stem: The anterior (rostral) neuropore normally closes at about day
questions.why: The anterior neuropore closes around day 25-26; the posterior neuropore closes about two days later.

questions.stem: Failure of the anterior neuropore to close results in
questions.why: Non-closure of the anterior neuropore gives anencephaly; non-closure of the posterior neuropore gives spina bifida.

questions.stem: Failure of the posterior (caudal) neuropore to close results in
questions.why: Non-closure of the posterior neuropore gives spina bifida, with defective vertebral arches.

questions.stem: Maternal deficiency of which vitamin is strongly associated with neural tube defects?
questions.why: Folate (vitamin B9) deficiency increases the risk of neural tube defects, so periconceptional supplementation is advised.

questions.stem: The three primary brain vesicles, from cranial to caudal, are the prosencephalon, mesencephalon and
questions.why: The three primary vesicles are the prosencephalon (forebrain), mesencephalon (midbrain) and rhombencephalon (hindbrain).

questions.stem: The cerebral hemispheres develop from the
questions.why: The prosencephalon forms the telencephalon (cerebral hemispheres) and the diencephalon (thalamus and optic vesicles).

questions.stem: The optic vesicles grow out from the
questions.why: The diencephalon gives rise to the optic vesicles as well as the thalamus and hypothalamus.

questions.stem: The cerebellum and pons develop from the
questions.why: The rhombencephalon forms the metencephalon (pons and cerebellum) and the myelencephalon (medulla).

questions.stem: The medulla oblongata develops from the
questions.why: The myelencephalon becomes the medulla oblongata, continuous with the spinal cord.

questions.stem: In the developing spinal cord the mantle layer becomes the
questions.why: The mantle layer (neuronal cell bodies) becomes grey matter; the outer marginal layer becomes white matter.

questions.stem: The motor neurons of the spinal cord develop in the
questions.why: The ventral basal plates form motor (efferent) neurons; the dorsal alar plates form sensory (afferent) neurons.

questions.stem: The sensory association neurons of the spinal cord develop in the
questions.why: The alar plates (dorsal) form sensory neurons; the basal plates (ventral) form motor neurons, separated by the sulcus limitans.

questions.stem: Which neuroglial cell type is NOT derived from neuroectoderm?
questions.why: Astrocytes, oligodendrocytes and ependyma arise from neuroectoderm; microglia come from mesenchyme (monocyte lineage).

questions.stem: In the adult the spinal cord typically ends at the level of
questions.why: Differential growth means the cord ends at about L3 at birth and L1 in the adult.

questions.stem: The oblique nerve roots and filum terminale at the lower end of the vertebral canal form the
questions.why: Below the conus the lumbosacral roots and filum terminale form the cauda equina.

questions.stem: Myelination of axons in the central nervous system is carried out by
questions.why: Oligodendrocytes myelinate CNS axons; Schwann cells myelinate peripheral axons.

questions.stem: Which process of brain development removes under-used synaptic connections?
questions.why: Pruning weeds out underused connections and strengthens frequently used ones, mostly between about ages 3 and 16.

questions.stem: The limb buds first appear during week
questions.why: Limb buds appear on the ventrolateral body wall in week 4; forelimb buds appear slightly before hindlimb buds.

questions.stem: The core of each limb bud is formed from
questions.why: Somatic lateral plate mesoderm forms the limb bud core (bones and connective tissue); muscle comes later from somites.

questions.stem: Outgrowth of the limb bud is initiated by which signalling molecule from the lateral plate mesoderm?
questions.why: FGF10 from the lateral plate mesoderm triggers limb bud outgrowth.

questions.stem: The thickened ectoderm at the tip of the limb bud is the
questions.why: The apical ectodermal ridge (AER) caps the bud and controls proximo-distal outgrowth via FGF8.

questions.stem: The apical ectodermal ridge controls patterning along which axis?
questions.why: The AER drives proximo-distal patterning (shoulder to fingertip); the ZPA controls antero-posterior patterning.

questions.stem: The zone of polarising activity determines digit identity by secreting
questions.why: The ZPA at the posterior margin secretes SHH, which patterns the antero-posterior (thumb to little-finger) axis.

questions.stem: Dorsal identity of the limb (back of the hand) is specified by
questions.why: Wnt7a from dorsal ectoderm specifies dorsal fate; Engrailed-1 from ventral ectoderm specifies ventral fate.

questions.stem: From proximal to distal, the limb skeleton forms in the order stylopod, zeugopod and
questions.why: Stylopod (humerus/femur), then zeugopod (radius-ulna/tibia-fibula), then autopod (hand/foot).

questions.stem: The humerus and femur correspond to which limb segment?
questions.why: The stylopod is the proximal segment (humerus in the arm, femur in the leg).

questions.stem: Positioning of the limbs along the cranio-caudal axis is governed by
questions.why: HOX (homeobox) genes set the cranio-caudal position at which limbs form.

questions.stem: Forelimb (versus hindlimb) identity is specified by which transcription factor?
questions.why: TBX5 (with FGF10) specifies the forelimb; TBX4 (with FGF10) specifies the hindlimb.

questions.stem: By week 6 the flattened ends of the limb buds are called
questions.why: The limb buds flatten into hand and foot plates by week 6.

questions.stem: Separation of the digits occurs by
questions.why: Programmed cell death (apoptosis) removes the interdigital mesenchyme, freeing the fingers and toes.

questions.stem: The muscles of the limbs are derived from
questions.why: Myogenic cells migrate into the limb bud from the somites; the bones form from somatic lateral plate mesoderm.

questions.stem: The bones of the limbs form by
questions.why: Mesenchyme forms hyaline cartilage models that are replaced by bone through endochondral ossification; ossification centres appear about week 12.

questions.stem: During week 7 the upper limbs rotate so that the thumb comes to lie
questions.why: The upper limbs rotate 90 degrees laterally (thumb lateral); the lower limbs rotate medially (big toe medial).

questions.stem: During week 7 the lower limbs rotate so that the great toe comes to lie
questions.why: The lower limbs rotate 90 degrees medially, placing the great toe medially and the extensors anteriorly.

questions.stem: The upper limb buds lie opposite which spinal segments?
questions.why: The upper limb buds lie opposite the lower five cervical and upper two thoracic segments (C5-T2).

questions.stem: Thalidomide causes limb defects mainly by
questions.why: Thalidomide inhibits angiogenesis in the developing limb, producing phocomelia and amelia.

questions.stem: Complete absence of a limb is termed
questions.why: Amelia is total absence of a limb; meromelia is partial absence; phocomelia is absence of proximal parts with the hand/foot attached near the trunk.

questions.stem: Fusion of adjacent digits is called
questions.why: Syndactyly is fusion of digits (failed interdigital apoptosis); polydactyly is extra digits.

questions.stem: Extra digits (supernumerary fingers or toes) is termed
questions.why: Polydactyly is the presence of extra digits.
